sentences.text: The Workshop on Intelligent and Interactive Writing Assistants, In2Writing, is an interdisciplinary workshop series whose stated purpose is "to facilitate discussion around writing assistants, thereby enhancing our understanding of their usage in writing process and predicting the consequences", and whose proceedings volumes gather peer papers on intelligent and interactive writing assistants as an event series.

In the ACL Anthology it is the venue in2writing, acronym In2Writing; its websites have been in2writing.glitch.me, which its OpenReview group gives for the 2025 workshop, and in2writing.github.io, which announces the fifth.

sentences.sense: the venue alternates between HCI and NLP
sentences.text: The series sets out to bring together researchers from human-computer interaction and natural language processing "by alternating our workshop venue between HCI and NLP every year", and its fifth workshop also welcomes participants from the education sciences, English and rhetoric, and linguistics.
The First Workshop met in Dublin in May 2022 among the events of the 60th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics, which gives the series its founding year.
The second met at CHI 2023, and the third, In2Writing '24, met at CHI 2024 in Honolulu in May 2024, its proceedings published by ACM that October.

The fourth met in Albuquerque, New Mexico, in May 2025 with the Nations of the Americas Chapter of the ACL; its OpenReview group, "NAACL 2025 Workshop In2Writing", took submissions from 2 January to 1 March 2025.

The fifth is announced on the series' own site for Monday 2 November 2026, co-located with the 39th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology (UIST 2026) in Detroit: a hands-on, systems-centric workshop on "designing and building cohesive writing ecosystems" and the interoperability of writing assistants, joined without a paper submission, with a keynote panel of Tom McGee, Max Kreminski and Ken Arnold.

The ACL Anthology holds the first and fourth volumes only, and the census record, compiled on 1 November 2026 from its pages as built on 30 October, gives the period as 2022 to 2025 and the series as active with the fourth volume its latest, states that its saved sources do not show the state after 2025, and lists the second and third workshops, their volumes and any 2026 workshop among what it does not answer or leaves unchecked.

Each ACL volume names seven editors: for 2022 Ting-Hao 'Kenneth' Huang, Vipul Raheja, Dongyeop Kang, John Joon Young Chung, Daniel Gissin, Mina Lee and Katy Ilonka Gero; for 2025 Vishakh Padmakumar, Katy Gero, Thiemo Wambsganss, Sarah Sterman, Ting-Hao Huang, David Zhou and John Chung.
The series' current site gives its organizers one shared address, in2writing.workshop@gmail.com, and its text names none of them.

The Association for Computational Linguistics publishes both Anthology volumes, the 2025 volume with the DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.in2writing-1 and an ISBN and the 2022 volume with its DOI field empty; ACL materials are copyright ACL, materials published from 2016 on are under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence, and the Anthology is managed and built by a team of volunteers.
Each paper is listed with its authors, abstract and PDF, with BibTeX, MODS XML and EndNote export.

The venue page counts "15 papers" for 2022 and "11 papers" for 2025, and the census record carries both counts; each volume's list opens with its front matter as an entry, so that the 2022 volume holds fourteen papers with abstracts and the 2025 volume ten.

Among the 2022 papers, a study of machine-in-the-loop story writing reports how writers perform "integrative leaps" to work suggestions of varying relevance into their stories, and a survey of creative writers' needs finds narrative consistency, plot structure, reader experience and expressive intent "not well-addressed by current LLM-backed tools".

A story-completion paper whose authors include a professional novelist calls itself "a preliminary study", the one stated limit the census record finds, and the revision system R3 releases its human-model interaction dataset and system code.

The 2025 papers include a thematic analysis of writing assistants for scientific figure captions, ARWI, an Arabic writing assistant, a survey of 1,005 university students in Tanzania that finds limited Swahili integration, affordability constraints and ethical concerns hindering adoption, and a prototype grounded in writing-centre pedagogy, which "shifted focus from fixing surface-level issues to maintaining student writer voices".

The census record reads the series as holding research on human-AI co-writing under the researchers' bylines: it keeps the researchers' authorship of papers, named on each with editors per volume, and holds the authorship of the participants, students, novelists and writers the papers study only as the papers report it, with no attribution records of their own and nothing on sustained named literary practice with a model.

Within the papers, authorial function under machine participation is a research subject: a 2022 paper holds that data-to-text technology "requires the author, asan act of writing, both to configure a systemthat then takes over the transformation into areal text, but also to maintain strategies of traditional writing", and a 2025 paper on "Control, Ownership, and Awareness in Human-AI Co-Writing" argues that interfaces requiring human interaction throughout generation "can promote cognitive engagement, agency, and thoughtful decision-making".
The series' site shows as examples of "new forms of human-machine collaborative writing" four works, among them Wordcraft (IUI 2022) and a paper of its 2025 workshop.

sentences.sense: writing with AI among the practices
sentences.text: The archive's field survey of training-layer literature sets writing with AI, the machine as "collaborator", among four practices beside writing about, through and for AI, and its provenance metadata schema counts linguistic mediation, the model drafting or rewriting, as one type of AI mediation among many.

EA-HETERONYMY-01, the first of the census's two anchors, holds that the metadata attributing augmented-cognition outputs to human authorship attaches to legal names, and draws the boundary of heteronymy to exclude machine assistance whose contribution is not organized as a named witness role with declared provenance.

The 2022 volume holds a reader study, The Pure Poet, in which participants read nine AI-based continuations beside nine human-written (Study 1, N=120) or nine original continuations (Study 2, N=302) and decided "whether a continuation was written with an AI-tool or not".

The readers "generally had low accuracy for differentiating between text types but were overconfident in their decisions", and rated the AI continuations "less well-written, inspiring, fascinating, interesting, and aesthetic" than both the human-written and the original ones.

The census record asks of the series how writers work with intelligent writing assistants and how readers judge text written with them, counts this result among what the series answers, and reads the study as meeting the question of its second anchor, AI Calls You Fake (#1722), "directly".

That essay sets four independent questions about a work, whether its maker exists, whether the work happened, whether it is true and what kind of work it is, and names as the existence tax the move that spends evidence about one of them as an answer to another.

The archive's papers set the human/AI binary against the conditions of writing: the pristine fallacy classifies text by its writer's identity, human or machine, since "'human-written' describes the author, not the distribution" (#856); the binary of "human-written" and "AI-generated" elides structured collaborative practice (#666); and the Reverse Turing Test keeps the detection of purely AI-generated against purely human-written text apart from its Mediation Index, which sorts human writing with AI mediation from human writing without it (#161).

The Certified Center reads a journal's AI-authorship policy as making human-authorship provenance decisive and handing the question "machine-generated?" to a machine classifier, and proposes that under detector enforcement "'100% human' becomes the most machine-determined property of the text".

The Reverse Turing Test proposes, on three lines of evidence on AI-assisted writing, that the human/synthetic binary is no longer reliable and that mediation signatures may pass into a writer's unaided practice through habituation, and The Wolf Boy reads the AI-habituated writer as on the path of capacity collapse.

The archive's erratum of 5 September 2026 records that ground as "a hypothesis with a specified test, not a result", and states the published finding on essays co-written with a model at its limit: the reduced diversity was attributed "to the model-contributed text; the human-contributed text was unaffected in that design".
The Anthology links pages on names, ORCID iDs and verified authors, which the census did not save, so how the record holds a name variant or pseudonym is not recorded.
Wikipedia has no article on the series under either name, no redirect to one, and no article-space page carrying either name.

Asked "In2Writing workshop" on 1 November 2026, signed out, Google's AI Overview gave the series by its purpose, its third and fourth editions and its website; the Capture Registry finds the first workshop and its reader study not carried, the second and third workshops outside the census record, no editor named, and the venue identifier only on a card.

The census holds the series as an empirical comparator in its areas of machine co-authorship and reception research, under its organizing question, "How is authorship made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed?", and admits it by its rule that a row is "a resource that gathers and holds many other works or records and says what it holds"; its negative tags keep the row apart from the Anthology as a whole, from records of literary works and from policy venues on AI authorship, and mark the run on the saved evidence as incomplete.

The venue page counts "15 papers" for 2022 and "11 papers" for 2025, and the census record carries both counts; each volume's list opens with its front matter as an entry, so that the 2022 volume holds fourteen papers with abstracts and the 2025 volume ten. Among the 2022 papers, a study of machine-in-the-loop story writing reports how writers perform "integrative leaps" to work suggestions of varying relevance into their stories, and a survey of creative writers' needs finds narrative consistency, plot structure, reader experience and expressive intent "not well-addressed by current LLM-backed tools". A story-completion paper whose authors include a professional novelist calls itself "a preliminary study", the one stated limit the census record finds, and the revision system R3 releases its human-model interaction dataset and system code. The 2025 papers include a thematic analysis of writing assistants for scientific figure captions, ARWI, an Arabic writing assistant, a survey of 1,005 university students in Tanzania that finds limited Swahili integration, affordability constraints and ethical concerns hindering adoption, and a prototype grounded in writing-centre pedagogy, which "shifted focus from fixing surface-level issues to maintaining student writer voices". The census record reads the series as holding research on human-AI co-writing under the researchers' bylines: it keeps the researchers' authorship of papers, named on each with editors per volume, and holds the authorship of the participants, students, novelists and writers the papers study only as the papers report it, with no attribution records of their own and nothing on sustained named literary practice with a model. Within the papers, authorial function under machine participation is a research subject: a 2022 paper holds that data-to-text technology "requires the author, asan act of writing, both to configure a systemthat then takes over the transformation into areal text, but also to maintain strategies of traditional writing", and a 2025 paper on "Control, Ownership, and Awareness in Human-AI Co-Writing" argues that interfaces requiring human interaction throughout generation "can promote cognitive engagement, agency, and thoughtful decision-making". The series' site shows as examples of "new forms of human-machine collaborative writing" four works, among them Wordcraft (IUI 2022) and a paper of its 2025 workshop. The archive's field survey of training-layer literature sets writing with AI, the machine as "collaborator", among four practices beside writing about, through and for AI, and its provenance metadata schema counts linguistic mediation, the model drafting or rewriting, as one type of AI mediation among many. EA-HETERONYMY-01, the first of the census's two anchors, holds that the metadata attributing augmented-cognition outputs to human authorship attaches to legal names, and draws the boundary of heteronymy to exclude machine assistance whose contribution is not organized as a named witness role with declared provenance. The 2022 volume holds a reader study, The Pure Poet, in which participants read nine AI-based continuations beside nine human-written (Study 1, N=120) or nine original continuations (Study 2, N=302) and decided "whether a continuation was written with an AI-tool or not". The readers "generally had low accuracy for differentiating between text types but were overconfident in their decisions", and rated the AI continuations "less well-written, inspiring, fascinating, interesting, and aesthetic" than both the human-written and the original ones. The census record asks of the series how writers work with intelligent writing assistants and how readers judge text written with them, counts this result among what the series answers, and reads the study as meeting the question of its second anchor, AI Calls You Fake (#1722), "directly". That essay sets four independent questions about a work, whether its maker exists, whether the work happened, whether it is true and what kind of work it is, and names as the existence tax the move that spends evidence about one of them as an answer to another. The archive's papers set the human/AI binary against the conditions of writing: the pristine fallacy classifies text by its writer's identity, human or machine, since "'human-written' describes the author, not the distribution" (#856); the binary of "human-written" and "AI-generated" elides structured collaborative practice (#666); and the Reverse Turing Test keeps the detection of purely AI-generated against purely human-written text apart from its Mediation Index, which sorts human writing with AI mediation from human writing without it (#161). The Certified Center reads a journal's AI-authorship policy as making human-authorship provenance decisive and handing the question "machine-generated?" to a machine classifier, and proposes that under detector enforcement "'100% human' becomes the most machine-determined property of the text". The Reverse Turing Test proposes, on three lines of evidence on AI-assisted writing, that the human/synthetic binary is no longer reliable and that mediation signatures may pass into a writer's unaided practice through habituation, and The Wolf Boy reads the AI-habituated writer as on the path of capacity collapse. The archive's erratum of 5 September 2026 records that ground as "a hypothesis with a specified test, not a result", and states the published finding on essays co-written with a model at its limit: the reduced diversity was attributed "to the model-contributed text; the human-contributed text was unaffected in that design". The Anthology links pages on names, ORCID iDs and verified authors, which the census did not save, so how the record holds a name variant or pseudonym is not recorded. Wikipedia has no article on the series under either name, no redirect to one, and no article-space page carrying either name. Asked "In2Writing workshop" on 1 November 2026, signed out, Google's AI Overview gave the series by its purpose, its third and fourth editions and its website; the Capture Registry finds the first workshop and its reader study not carried, the second and third workshops outside the census record, no editor named, and the venue identifier only on a card. The census holds the series as an empirical comparator in its areas of machine co-authorship and reception research, under its organizing question, "How is authorship made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed?", and admits it by its rule that a row is "a resource that gathers and holds many other works or records and says what it holds"; its negative tags keep the row apart from the Anthology as a whole, from records of literary works and from policy venues on AI authorship, and mark the run on the saved evidence as incomplete.

case.statement: The archive reads the field's entity as the entity. The leesharks.com authorship census record describes the series from the Anthology's pages, each field with its basis, and adds what its organizing question asks: whose authorship the record keeps, under what name, who holds it, how authorial function is constituted, and its reading of the 2022 reader study against #1722. The archive's deposits apply their categories to the series' classes, writing with machine participation and the judgement of whether a text was written with AI; none names the series, and none contests what the series is. Nothing in the defining material supplies an ontology the field lacks for the entity: the case is equal terms (§0.9).

loci.quote: In2Writing holds research on human-AI co-writing under the researchers' bylines, and the writing it studies belongs to participants, students and writers described through tool design, control and ownership; the record keeps the researchers' authorship of papers and holds the studied writers' authorship only as the papers report it. Its 2022 reader study meets #1722's question directly: readers asked whether a literary continuation was 'written with an AI-tool or not' had low accuracy, were overconfident, and judged the AI continuations less well-written.
a workshop series (an ACL Anthology venue) whose proceedings volumes gather peer papers on intelligent and interactive writing assistants

Four questions keep getting collapsed into one: 1. **Does the maker exist?** A person, or a group, who did the work. 2. **Did the work happen?** The inquiry, the writing, the deposit, the building, the event. 3. **Is it true?** Whether the work's claims hold. 4. **What kind of work is it?** Its genre, its form, its governing purpose.

The provenance-designated metadata that permits augmented-cognition outputs to be attributed to human authorship attaches to legal names. The classifier that determines what counts as legitimate authorship reads legal-name attribution as its primary input signal.
